title: Polar Form of a Complex Number
short: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ).

blocks.html: A point in the complex plane can be described by its distance and angle as well as by its coordinates, just like polar coordinates. For complex numbers this polar description makes multiplication remarkably simple, as the next lesson shows.

$$z = a + bi = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta),$$ where $r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ is the modulus and $\theta$ is the argument, the angle from the positive real axis (with $\tan\theta = \frac{b}{a}$ in the right quadrant). Going back: $a = r\cos\theta$, $b = r\sin\theta$. Some books write $r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ for short.
$z$ is the point $(a, b)$. Its polar coordinates are $(r, \theta)$ with $a = r\cos\theta$ and $b = r\sin\theta$, so $$a + bi = r\cos\theta + ir\sin\theta = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta).$$

blocks.cap: With polar marks on, the readout gives the modulus and argument of $z$.

blocks.title: To polar form
steps: The point $(-1, \sqrt{3})$ is in Quadrant II with reference angle $\frac{\pi}{3}$ (since $\tan = \sqrt{3}$), so $\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$.

blocks.title: Back to $a + bi$
blocks.q: Write $4\left(\cos\frac{7\pi}{4} + i\sin\frac{7\pi}{4}\right)$ in the form $a + bi$.

blocks.title: On an axis
steps: It is the point $(0, -3)$: distance $3$, straight down.

blocks.html: Reading the argument off a calculator's $\tan^{-1}\frac{b}{a}$ without checking the quadrant, the same trap as with polar coordinates. For $-1 + i\sqrt{3}$ that gives $-\frac{\pi}{3}$, which points into Quadrant IV. Plot the point first.
